title: Towards Better Decodables and Better Use of Decodables
author: Timothy Shanahan
summary: Timothy Shanahan revisits a core assumption of systematic phonics instruction — that decodable texts, giving students concentrated practice with a specific letter-sound pattern, are an unambiguous good — and finds the research base thinner and more cautionary than commonly assumed. He notes that direct studies of decodables find only fleeting benefits and that by the end of first grade researchers can no longer distinguish students who used decodables from those who didn't, which alone should temper enthusiasm. His more original argument draws on 'statistical learning' theory: because decodable texts deliberately over-represent one spelling pattern far beyond its natural frequency in English (packing a text with CVCe words, for instance), they can misteach children about how consistently that pattern actually predicts pronunciation, with documented long-term effects on decoding flexibility. To demonstrate a fix rather than just a critique, Shanahan has ChatGPT generate two decodable stories, then revises both to deliberately insert common high-frequency words that break the target pattern (like 'come' and 'have' alongside CVCe words), arguing this keeps students honest about the real inconsistency of English spelling rather than training false confidence in one pattern. He grounds this in established word-study principles from Words Their Way — 'compare words that "do" with words that "don't"' and 'don't hide exceptions' — concluding that good decodable practice should deliberately include exceptions requiring genuine choice, not just rote, artificially consistent repetition.
points: Shanahan's statistical-learning argument — that decodable texts 'skew the statistical properties of English' by over-representing one pattern, misleading children about its real-world consistency — reframes decodables from a pure benefit into a tool with a specific, correctable design flaw.

His concrete revision technique, deliberately inserting common exception words like 'come' and 'have' into otherwise pattern-heavy decodable texts, gives teachers and curriculum writers an immediately usable fix rather than an abstract critique.

Citing Words Their Way's principles 'compare words that "do" with words that "don't"' and 'don't hide exceptions' connects his specific concern about decodables to an established, broader framework for word study, strengthening the argument beyond a single researcher's opinion.
quotes: There has been surprisingly little research on the benefits of decodables in teaching reading.
By the end of grade 1, one can't tell if students worked with decodables or not (Juel & Roper-Schneider, 1985).

Decodable texts aim to provide students with intensive practice with specific decoding patterns, so they skew the statistical properties of English—increasing the presence of a pattern well beyond what it typically appears in text.
Studies show long term repercussions from over representing a pattern in early instructional texts (Venezky & Johnson, 1973).

I worked done and come into the first story and have into the second—high frequency words that break the pattern. Including such rule breakers in decodables, keeps kids honest and gives them a better idea what decoding requires.
Two of the 11 principles are relevant here: 'Compare words that 'do' with words that 'don't'' and 'Don't hide exceptions.''
Decodables should do more than provide intensive concentrated practice, they should introduce inconsistencies that will require choice rather than rote responses.
